steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper presenting METAVerse, a meta-learning framework that learns a LiDAR-based terrain traversability cost map for off-road navigation and adapts it online.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Terrain traversability in off-road navigation and why it is hard
2. Self-supervised traversability learning from vehicle-terrain interaction
3. Limitation: epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty across environments
4. Our approach: METAVerse
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Off-road traversability
- diverse unstructured terrains, distinct characteristics
- safe, stable navigation needs predicting vehicle-terrain interaction on upcoming trajectory
- predicted difficulty = traversability; key for local path planning and control
- hard to estimate accurately with limited sensors
- human-annotated datasets -> semantic classifier, but unseen and ambiguous terrains -> inaccurate
- same terrain class can differ in traversability; complex properties not captured by manual labels

2. Self-supervised approaches
- use vehicle-terrain interaction from real navigation to learn traversability
- map exteroceptive data (RGB, LiDAR point clouds) -> cost defined by interaction measured with proprioceptive sensors (IMU)
- continuous-valued cost maps represent difficulty precisely
- reflect vehicle capabilities + terrain characteristics from real experience -> better navigation

3. Limitation
- don't generalize; hard to get global model for many environments
- supervision only where vehicle interacted -> high epistemic uncertainty on unexplored terrain
- even with varied data: substantial aleatoric uncertainty
- traversability depends on many interconnected factors (platform, geometry, deformability, bumpiness, friction, roughness)
- subtle variations not captured by limited sensors; similar geometry, very different ground-truth traversability
- result: imprecise predictions, nothing more nuanced than terrain classification, suboptimal navigation

4. METAVerse
- meta-learning-based framework for learning terrain traversability; global model across off-road environments
- training: network predicts dense, continuous-valued cost map in real time from single sweep LiDAR point clouds
- meta-learning finds initial parameters that generalize with a few gradient descent steps
- deployment: quick adaptation to local context using recent vehicle-terrain interactions
- real-world driving data on varied unstructured terrains -> reduced uncertainty
- integration with sampling-based model predictive controller -> stable, safe navigation
- overview Fig. 1

5. Contributions
- deep meta-learning framework, global network, dense cost map from sparse LiDAR
- online adaptation from navigation experience to minimize uncertainty
- reduced prediction uncertainty on data from various terrains
- stable navigation with sampling-based MPC

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In off-road navigation, autonomous vehicles run into many different unstructured terrains, each with distinct characteristics. For safe and stable navigation in off-road environments, the vehicle needs to predict how it will interact with the terrain in the upcoming trajectory. The predicted difficulty of this interaction, which is the traversability of the terrain, plays a critical role in different navigation strategies such as local path planning and control. But it is challenging to estimate terrain traversability accurately in off-road environments with limited sensors. Human-annotated datasets can be used to train a semantic classifier, but off-road environments are full of unseen and ambiguous terrains, so the traversability predictions are inaccurate. Also, terrains from the same terrain class can have different degrees of traversability because their traversability-related properties are complex and variable, and manually labeled data cannot capture this.

Recently off-road navigation has gained a lot from self-supervised approaches that use vehicle-terrain interaction from actual navigation experience to learn terrain traversability. These methods learn a mapping from exteroceptive data (e.g., RGB and LiDAR point clouds) to a traversability cost, which is defined by the vehicle-terrain interaction measured with proprioceptive sensors (e.g., Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)). The traversability cost maps they produce have continuous-valued scores and can represent the difficulty of navigation precisely. These cost maps also reflect the vehicle's navigation capabilities and the terrain characteristics from actual experience, so navigation performance is better.

[Limitation of self-supervised methods]
- no generalization; global model hard
- supervision only where vehicle interacted -> high epistemic uncertainty for unexplored terrain
- aleatoric uncertainty remains even with varied data
- many interconnected factors (platform, geometry, deformability, bumpiness, friction, roughness); limited sensors can't capture subtle variations
- similar geometry, very different ground-truth traversability -> imprecise, no better than terrain classification

[METAVerse]
- meta-learning-based, global model for various off-road environments
- dense continuous cost map in real time from single sweep LiDAR
- meta-learning: initial parameters generalizing in a few gradient steps
- online adaptation from recent vehicle-terrain interactions
- real-world data shows reduced uncertainty; sampling-based MPC -> stable, safe navigation; Fig. 1

[Contributions]
- meta-learning framework, dense cost map from sparse LiDAR
- online adaptation to minimize uncertainty
- reduced uncertainty on varied terrain data
- stable navigation with sampling-based MPC

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In off-road navigation, autonomous vehicles run into many different unstructured terrains, each with distinct characteristics. For safe and stable navigation in off-road environments, the vehicle needs to predict how it will interact with the terrain in the upcoming trajectory. The predicted difficulty of this interaction, which is the traversability of the terrain, plays a critical role in different navigation strategies such as local path planning and control. But it is challenging to estimate terrain traversability accurately in off-road environments with limited sensors. Human-annotated datasets can be used to train a semantic classifier, but off-road environments are full of unseen and ambiguous terrains, so the traversability predictions are inaccurate. Also, terrains from the same terrain class can have different degrees of traversability because their traversability-related properties are complex and variable, and manually labeled data cannot capture this.

Recently off-road navigation has gained a lot from self-supervised approaches that use vehicle-terrain interaction from actual navigation experience to learn terrain traversability. These methods learn a mapping from exteroceptive data (e.g., RGB and LiDAR point clouds) to a traversability cost, which is defined by the vehicle-terrain interaction measured with proprioceptive sensors (e.g., Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)). The traversability cost maps they produce have continuous-valued scores and can represent the difficulty of navigation precisely. These cost maps also reflect the vehicle's navigation capabilities and the terrain characteristics from actual experience, so navigation performance is better.

However these methods do not generalize to various environments, since it is hard to get a global model that works reliably in many environments. The interaction data only gives supervision for the regions the vehicle has interacted with, so the model's predictions for unexplored terrain have high epistemic uncertainty. And even if interaction data is collected on a variety of terrains to reduce epistemic uncertainty, the model's estimation still has a lot of aleatoric uncertainty. In real-world off-road environments, terrain traversability is influenced by many interconnected and complex factors (e.g., platform, geometry, deformability, bumpiness, friction, and roughness). But these subtle variations cannot be captured precisely with a limited sensor configuration. The geometric characteristics of the terrain captured by a sensor might look similar while the ground-truth traversability varies a lot, and this gives a high level of aleatoric uncertainty. Because of these uncertainties the predictions are less precise, and it is impossible to estimate traversability costs that are more nuanced than simple terrain classification, which leads to suboptimal off-road navigation performance.

This paper presents a meta-learning-based framework for learning terrain traversability (METAVerse), which can learn a global model that predicts terrain traversability accurately in various off-road environments. In training, the traversability cost prediction network learns to generate a dense, continuous-valued cost map in real-time from single sweep LiDAR point clouds. To minimize the uncertainty of the network trained with data from many different terrains, we use meta-learning to find initial network parameters that generalize well with a few gradient descent steps. In deployment, the model quickly adapts to the local context with gradient descents using the recent history of vehicle-terrain interactions, which allows effective off-road navigation. We show with real-world driving data collected on unstructured terrains with varying properties that our method can learn a global model that reduces prediction uncertainty. We also integrate our framework with a sampling-based model predictive controller and show that our method helps stable and safe navigation in unstructured environments. Fig. 1 shows an overview of our framework.

To summarize, the main contributions of our work are:

- We introduce a deep meta-learning framework to learn a global terrain traversability prediction network that can reliably produce a dense cost map from a sparse LiDAR point cloud in various environments.

- We propose a method that minimizes estimation uncertainty by adapting the network online based on the vehicle's navigation experience.

- We show that our method can reduce prediction uncertainty using data collected in various terrains.

- We validate that our method gives stable navigation by integrating our traversability cost map with a sampling-based model predictive controller.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
During off-road navigation, autonomous vehicles encounter diverse unstructured terrains with distinct characteristics. To ensure safe and stable navigation in off-road environments, it is necessary to predict the interaction of a vehicle with the terrains in an upcoming trajectory [1]. The predicted difficulty of interaction, which represents the traversability of the terrain, plays a critical role in various navigational strategies such as local path planning and control [2,3]. However, accurately estimating terrain traversability in off-road environments with limited sensors is challenging. Even though human-annotated datasets can be used to train a semantic classifier, off-road environments are full of unseen and ambiguous terrains, which results in inaccurate traversability predictions. Moreover, terrains of the same terrain class may have varying degrees of traversability due to their complex and variable traversability-related properties, which manually labeled data cannot capture.

Recently, off-road navigation has benefited significantly from self-supervised approaches that use the vehicle-terrain interaction of actual navigation experiences to learn terrain traversability [4,5,6]. These methods learn a mapping from exteroceptive data (e.g., RGB and LiDAR point clouds) to a traversability cost defined by the vehicle-terrain interaction measured with proprioceptive sensors (e.g., Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)). The resulting traversability cost maps, with continuous-valued scores, can precisely represent the difficulty of navigation. Moreover, these cost maps reflect the navigation capabilities of a vehicle and the terrain characteristics based on actual experiences, resulting in enhanced navigational performance.

However, these methods cannot be generalized to various environments, since it is challenging to acquire a global model that operates reliably in numerous environments. As the interaction data only provides supervision for regions the vehicle has interacted with, the model's predictions for unexplored terrains are subject to high epistemic uncertainty [7]. Even if interaction data are obtained on a variety of terrains to reduce epistemic uncertainty, the model's estimation is still subject to a substantial amount of aleatoric uncertainty. In real-world off-road environments, terrain traversability is intricately influenced by a multitude of interconnected and complex factors (e.g., platform, geometry, deformability, bumpiness, friction, and roughness) [8]. Such subtle variations cannot be captured precisely with a limited sensor configuration: while the geometric characteristics of the terrain captured by a sensor may be comparable, its ground-truth traversability can vary considerably, resulting in a high level of aleatoric uncertainty. These uncertainties lead to less precise predictions and make it impossible to estimate traversability costs more nuanced than simple terrain classification, resulting in suboptimal off-road navigational performance.

This paper presents a meta-learning-based framework for learning terrain traversability (METAVerse), which is capable of learning a global model that accurately predicts terrain traversability in various off-road environments. During training, the traversability cost prediction network learns to generate a dense, continuous-valued cost map in real-time from single sweep LiDAR point clouds. To minimize the uncertainty of the network trained with data collected from various terrains, meta-learning is used to discover initial network parameters that enable effective generalization with a few gradient descent steps. During deployment, the model quickly adapts to the local context with gradient descents based on the recent history of vehicle-terrain interactions, allowing for effective off-road navigation. Using real-world driving data collected on unstructured terrains with varying properties, we demonstrate that our method can learn a global model that reduces prediction uncertainty. In addition, by integrating our framework with a sampling-based model predictive controller, we demonstrate that our method facilitates stable and safe navigation in unstructured environments. An overview of our framework is presented in Fig. 1.

In summary, the main contributions of our work are:

- We introduce a deep meta-learning framework for learning a global terrain traversability prediction network that can reliably generate a dense cost map from a sparse LiDAR point cloud in various environments.

- We propose a method to minimize estimation uncertainty by adapting the network online based on the vehicle's navigation experience.

- We demonstrate that our method can reduce prediction uncertainty using data collected in various terrains.

- We validate that our method leads to stable navigation by integrating our traversability cost map with a sampling-based model predictive controller.

References:

[2] D. D. Fan, A.-A. Agha-Mohammadi, and E. A. Theodorou, “Learning risk-aware costmaps for traversability in challenging environments,” IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters , vol. 7, no. 1, pp. 279–286, 2021.
[3] J. Frey, D. Hoeller, S. Khattak, and M. Hutter, “Locomotion policy guided traversability learning using volumetric representations of complex environments,” in IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , 2022, pp. 5722–5729.
[4] D. Kim, J. Sun, S. M. Oh, J. M. Rehg, and A. F. Bobick, “Traversability classification using unsupervised on-line visual learning for outdoor robot navigation,” in IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) , 2006, pp. 518–525.
[5] J. Zürn, W. Burgard, and A. Valada, “Self-supervised visual terrain classification from unsupervised acoustic feature learning,” IEEE Transactions on Robotics , vol. 37, no. 2, pp. 466–481, 2020.
